terms.comment: The everyday verb for going anywhere. Where to is the accusative alone for towns and small islands and for domum and rūs (Rōmam īre, domum īre, rūs īre); otherwise ad or in with the accusative (ad avum, in hortum). An errand takes the supine: cubitum, dormītum, lūsum īre (Hor. S. 1.5.48; 1.6.119). “Let’s go!” is Eāmus!

terms.gloss: go, make one’s way (with purpose or haste)
terms.register: vōx in ōrātiōne solūtā rāra (Cic. Att., Liv.); apud poētās (Verg.) et in Vulgātā frequēns
evidence: Cic. Att. 4.10.2: ad eum postrīdiē māne vādēbam
Vulg. Lc. 10.37: Vāde, et tū fac similiter
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “rare but classical”. No classical perfect.

phrases.english: Up you get, lover boy, and go home.

phrases.latin: C. Arrius proximus est vīcīnus, immō ille quidem jam contubernālis, quī etiam sē idcircō Rōmam īre negat ut hīc mēcum tōtōs diēs philosophētur.
phrases.english: Gaius Arrius is my nearest neighbour, or rather my housemate by now: he even says he isn’t going to Rome, so that he can spend whole days here philosophising with me.

phrases.latin: dormīre quotiēns libuit, īmus ad vīllam
phrases.english: whenever I want to sleep, I go off to my house in the country

phrases.latin: Ego rūs ībō, atque ibi manēbō.
phrases.english: I’ll go to the country and stay there.
